So should a PM just rely on their own dog fooding of the product and their own walkthrough to figure out how to fix it? And a couple of times recently this has come up, and I think the consensus seems to be, "Yes, this is a good thing." And I have a contrarian opinion there, too, which is that I think it is really important for everyone to dog food their own products. The problem is related to relying on your intuition about those products, which is the thing most PMs have trouble with is realizing, "You are nothing like the user. You are nothing like them in ways that will bias the way you think about what's good and bad in your product in ways that you can't necessarily recognize. Some things with a product, some problems with a product, you need a pulse to recognize." (01:07:57): And most good PMs that I know have a pulse and so cool. But a lot of them require context of use, priorities, constraints that you just don't have and you can't imagine purely on the basis of your own usage. So what I think that means is that you should definitely dog food your own product. Doing product walkthroughs to identify lists of potential issues is a great thing to do. Prioritizing that list, figuring out which ones are more or less a problem, and for whom is an area where you should be extremely wary of relying on your own opinion, expertise, or intuition when you are dog fooding your own product.
turns.zh: 我能问个问题吗？好的，我还想补充一点，因为这个话题最近在你的播客里被提过几次，那就是关于产品经理自己测试产品的想法。所以产品经理是否应该完全依赖自己对产品的体验和演示来找出问题所在呢？最近这个话题被多次提起，我觉得大家的共识似乎是“是的，这是一件好事”。但我对此持相反意见，我认为每个人都应该亲自测试自己的产品很重要。问题在于依赖自己对产品的直觉，这是大多数产品经理都遇到的难题——他们意识到：“你和用户完全不同。你和他们的差异会影响你对产品优缺点的判断，而这些判断可能并非你所能意识到的。有些产品问题，只有亲自使用才能发现。”（01:07:57）：我认识的大多数优秀产品经理都具备这种洞察力，这很棒。但很多产品经理缺乏使用场景、优先级和约束条件的背景，而这些都是你仅凭自身使用无法想象的。所以我的观点是，你绝对应该亲自测试自己的产品。通过产品演示来识别潜在问题列表是一件很棒的事。但优先处理这些问题、判断哪些问题更严重、针对哪些用户群体时，你要格外警惕，不要依赖自己的观点、专业知识或直觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you for sharing that. It's definitely come up a bunch on this podcast, so I think that's an important lesson for people to take away. Anything else before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 感谢你分享这些。这话题在播客里确实被提过很多次，所以我觉得这是大家应该记住的重要经验。接下来进入激动人心的闪电问答环节前，你还有什么想说的吗？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: I appreciate you, Lenny. Thanks for having me on.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Lenny。感谢邀请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate you, Judd. Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我很感激你，Judd。好的，接下来就进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: I recently read a business book by Barbara Kellerman called Bad Leadership. And what I love about it is that we spend a lot of time talking about good leaders, and she really dives into the worst leaders and what makes them bad leaders in a way that I think is really valuable for everybody. (01:09:19): I'd also recommend, I read a lot of fiction, so two recommendations, there. One, a recent Pulitzer Prize winner, Demon Copperhead by Barbara Kingsolver. It's an outstanding read that also is really sad, and moving, and illustrative, especially if you want to understand rural poverty. And then completely other side of the fiction spectrum, if you're interested in science fiction, which I am, read the Murderbot Diaries, it's about a sarcastic killer robot. And who doesn't love them?
turns.zh: 我最近读了芭芭拉·凯勒曼的一本商业书籍，叫《坏领导力》。我喜欢这本书的地方在于，我们花了很多时间谈论好领导者，而她真正深入探讨了最糟糕的领导者，以及他们糟糕的原因，我认为这对每个人都非常有价值。（01:09:19）：我还推荐两本小说。一本是最近的普利策奖得主作品，芭芭拉·金索弗的《恶魔铜头》。它是一本杰出的读物，也非常悲伤、感人且具有启示意义，特别是如果你想了解农村贫困问题。然后是另一个完全相反的小说领域，如果你对科幻感兴趣的话，我推荐《谋杀机器人日记》，讲的是一个爱讽刺人的杀人机器人。谁不喜欢这样的角色呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love these fiction recommendations. I feel like we need more of these on the podcast, so thank you.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这些小说推荐。我觉得播客里需要更多这样的内容，所以谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Yeah. Everybody goes to business books.
turns.zh: 是啊。大家都去读商业书籍了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 是的，绝对的。你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: We recently watched The Last of Us and it blew our mind. I watched it after I played the video game after long last, if you are a person who plays video games and you haven't played The Last of Us, play it. If you don't know, the show is based on the video game, not the other way around.
turns.zh: 我们最近看了《最后生还者》，这部作品简直太震撼了。我是在很久没玩这款游戏后才看的剧集。如果你也是个游戏玩家但还没玩过《最后生还者》，那一定要去玩一玩。顺便说一句，这部剧是基于游戏改编的，而不是反过来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question you like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 你有没有最喜欢问面试者的某个问题？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Think of a topic that you had to explain lately that was the most complex, and then explain it to me like I'm five. And there are a lot of ways to vary that question, but the reason I like it is because I think, and I've asked this question to VP and C-suite candidates in multiple disciplines, and sometimes it's related to a conversation, like I might ask them to explain something complicated about quantum computing, or music theory, or it could be a complex business decision, but I want to see if somebody can break a complex problem down in a really simple way, and give me an intuition for it in a short amount of time. I think that is a differentiator between good and great for many people.
turns.zh: 想想最近你解释过的最复杂的主题，然后用通俗易懂的语言给我讲一遍。当然，这个问题的变体有很多，但我喜欢这个问题的原因在于，我曾向不同领域的副总裁和高管候选人提过这个问题，话题有时与之前的对话相关，比如让他们解释量子计算或音乐理论的复杂之处，或者是复杂的商业决策。但我希望看到候选人能用简洁明了的方式拆解复杂问题，短时间内为我提供直观理解。我认为这对许多人而言，是区分优秀与卓越的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Yeah, this is a really weird one, but my whole family started indoor rock climbing recently, and there's a challenge you have when you top rope, which is that you're looking up all the time. So they make these glasses, which are called belay glasses, and they have an angled mirror embedded in the lens, so that you can look straight ahead, and the view you see is up towards the person who you're belaying. And I just thought that product is so perfect for that. That's a niche problem and there isn't a better way to solve it.
turns.zh: 是啊，这个问题听起来挺奇怪的，但我全家最近开始玩室内攀岩。在顶绳攀岩时，你得一直抬头看。这时候就有了专门的攀岩护目镜，镜片里嵌入了斜角镜，让你能直视前方，同时看到攀岩者的视角。我觉得这个产品设计得太贴心了。这是个小众需求，却找不到更好的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite motto that you often come back to, that you share with friends either in work or in life that you find useful?
turns.zh: 你有没有常挂在嘴边、在工作或生活中与朋友分享的座右铭？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Yeah. This is going to seem like pandering, Lenny, but I don't know if you remember a conversation that you and I had, it must've been eight years ago. I remember where we were sitting. And it was about stoicism. Do you remember this? Anyway, we had this conversation.
turns.zh: 有啊。这听起来有点讨巧，Lenny，但你应该还记得我们八年前的一次谈话吧？我记得当时我们坐在哪里。当时我们聊的是斯多葛主义。你记得吗？总之，我们讨论了这个话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't, but I was into stoicism for a while.
turns.zh: 我不记得了，但我当时确实对斯多葛主义感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: I know you were, because we talked about it. And so the motto comes from stoicism, which is basically, "Focus on the things you can control and ignore the rest." And a lot of people think of this as the serenity prayer or the serenity saying, that was a 20th century invention, but Epictetus was writing about this BC, and I think about it all the time. So much of the stress, and pain, and worry that we have in life comes from things we can't control. So I try to let those things go.
turns.zh: 我知道你感兴趣，因为我们聊过这个。斯多葛主义的座右铭是：“专注于你能控制的事，忽视其他。” 很多人把这句话和20世纪发明的“宁静祈祷”或“宁静宣言”联系起来，但埃皮克提图早在公元前就提出了这个观点。我时常思考它。生活中大部分的压力、痛苦和焦虑都来自我们无法控制的事。所以我尽量放下这些执念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I learned that lesson from 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, and just the importance of thinking about these circles of you can control, you can influence, and you have no control over, and there's no reason to think about those other things.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我从《高效能人士的7个习惯》中领悟到这一点，以及思考可控、可影响和不可控三种圈子的重要性，没必要去想其他事情。

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Judd, this was everything I hoped it would be. We got into some really good stuff. I'm excited to hear how people react. Two final questions, where can folks find you if they want to learn about what you're up to, actually share what you're up to these days, and how people can find you, and then also how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 贾德，这次访谈完全超出了我的预期。我们探讨了许多深刻的话题。我很期待听听听众们的反馈。最后两个问题：如果人们想了解你的最新动态，或者分享你的近况，可以通过哪些渠道找到你？另外，听众们如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Yeah. Thanks for asking those questions. People can find me at juddantin.com. That's the best way to find out what I'm up to. These days, I'm a consultant. I help people with UX strategy, org design, and crisis management. Somehow I love dealing with other people's dumpster fires, and I've found that I'm constitutionally good at it somehow. So juddantin.com is the place to find out. I also write. I write a medium post that you can find at onebigthought.com. And you'll find a lot of the topics we talked about today, including the original post that started this at onebigthought.com. If there's one thing I could ask your listeners to do is to get next to your researcher. I just think if you build those relationships and involve a researcher and insights person early and often, beautiful things will happen for you and for the business. So that's the thing everyone can do for me.
turns.zh: 是的。感谢你提这些问题。大家可以访问juddantin.com来联系我。这是了解我动态的最佳途径。目前我是一名顾问，专注于用户体验策略、组织设计和危机管理。不知为何，我特别喜欢帮助别人解决棘手的问题，而且发现自己在这方面天生就很擅长。所以想了解更多信息，请访问juddantin.com。我还写作呢，在Medium上开设专栏，网址是onebigthought.com。今天我们讨论的许多话题，包括引发这次对谈的原文，都能在那里找到。如果能请听众们帮我一个忙，那就是多与研究员合作。我坚信，如果尽早、频繁地让研究员和洞察团队参与其中，对个人和企业都会带来巨大价值。这就是每个人能为我做的最有价值的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I've always done that. I loved my researchers that I've worked with, many of them reporting to you, and so beautiful takeaway. Judd, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 这观点太棒了。我一直这么做。我很欣赏曾合作过的研究员，其中很多都向你汇报过，这真是宝贵的经验。贾德，非常感谢你今天的参与。

turns.speaker: Judd Antin
turns.en: Lenny, thank you. It's been a pleasure.
turns.zh: 莱尼，谢谢你。这次访谈很愉快。
